How the agent works a workstream

Whether the agent should open, shape and move a workstream’s arcs as this page shows, so the book and spn-devex say it next.

Today planning can look like building, arcs are cut by release or by repository, a landed arc gets reopened, and you are told about steps by number. This page shows the workstream as it would run instead: what the agent needs before it opens one, how arcs are shaped while you plan, which of your words move what, the three state machines, and every case. It ends with where the change lands.

Overview

You are asked to decide whether the workstream should run as § Proposed shows. It serves the approach page’s The agent spends its tokens on the change.

Look first at the arc’s status and the kinds of go, then read the cases: each one says what the agent does and what you would see.

Not final: the names review-fixes arc and wait are working names, and the cost targets are checked again on the next workstream. Delegated work in the light form is already built, and it is shown here so the whole way of working is on one page.

Today

A workstream runs on eight arc statuses, reading counted as building, and six tables that each place new work a different way.

What happens today, and what it causes

You see: an arc reading RUNNING while nothing is built, then flipping back

Talking to you

Proposed

At any moment you can tell what is being shaped, what you agreed, what is being built and what is done; everything you review is an arc with its preview, and the agent does the bookkeeping and tells you each move in one line.

What you see, and what stays the agent’s

  • You see the approach page, the arcs’ previews and the changes in the repositories. An arc is named by its number and title, because an arc is what you review.
  • The agent keeps its steps (the rows) and its briefs to children (the orders). Neither is ever cited to you by number: not on the approach page, a preview, a card, a suggestion or a reply.
  • A block is said in words: “the test sign-in on the provider page waits on the server change”, never “row 7 cannot proceed”.

The units

Unit

Workstream

One subject with one goal, created only when you and the agent agree. Its approach page holds the goal, Why, What (each decision as a statement), How (the arcs, and one line for each arc still expected) and Open (the cards).

Status: PLANNING · IMPLEMENTING · DONE · Folder: backlog/, open/ or closed/

Arc

What you review together on one preview and what releases together, named for the domain it lands in as the repository’s own concept names its domains; where a concept names none, the agent asks you. It says what will be true when it lands, and how that is proved.

Status: six, § Arc status

Step

One build step, in chain order: book, registers, repository docs, code, release. Only build steps are recorded; reading and drafting never are.

Status: the agent’s own, § The agent’s steps

Planning job

A read or a draft that prepares a preview, done by the agent itself, and by a child only when it would take more than about 15 minutes. What comes back is facts and the preview section, with no report file.

Status: none, ever

Build job

A light-form brief for build steps (§ Delegated work), only for judgement work of more than about 15 minutes.

Status: through its steps

Card

A choice that changes what gets built, in Open until you answer; the answer then becomes a statement in What and in the preview it touches.

Status: open · answered

Before a workstream exists: what the agent needs

You ask for a workstream, or the agent suggests one while you discuss something else and you agree. The agent reads what it can from disk first, never asks again for what you already said, and then asks two or three plain questions at a time until it can say these back to you in one block.

Base information

The subject

In a few words.

For 030: page patterns · Becomes: the folder name

The goal

What is true when it is done, for whom, and how we will know.

For 030: every page of our apps and sites follows a named pattern a partner can reuse; each page names its pattern, and the showcase shows each one · Becomes: the page’s subtitle, and the proof of the last arc

Why now

What goes wrong if nothing changes.

For 030: pages are built one by one, and each looks different · Becomes: Why

What it reaches

As far as is known: the domains, the apps, the sites.

For 030: the Surface standard, the design system, the platform’s apps, saasplane.ai · Becomes: the domains, and whether a partner is affected

What you want to see first

The thing you would review first, and in what form.

For 030: the patterns as a page of sketches · Becomes: N001 and its preview

Limits

What must not change, and what a release may be.

For 030: minor releases only; Launchpad’s apps stay as they are · Becomes: traps, and steps that are never written

It does not need the list of arcs, the steps or the sizes: shaping finds those. At your yes to the block, the agent creates the workstream at the next free number, writes its approach page from the block, and opens N001, the arc for what you want to see first, named for its domain, as PROPOSED with its preview. Each arc it expects beyond N001 is one line in How. From its first write the new workstream passes state check and the Stop hook, with N001 PROPOSED and no steps.

Shaping: arcs while you plan

  1. As the discussion makes things clear, an expected line in How becomes an arc with its own preview. The agent merges arcs that turn out to be reviewed together or that release the same package, and rewrites an arc’s goal when the discussion moves it. A preview section already written moves with the arc that takes it.
  2. An arc never decided is reshaped freely: renumbered, merged or deleted, with no history.
  3. Several arcs can be PROPOSED at once, and none is a placeholder: an arc opens only with a goal and a preview section you can read, or with its steps when there is nothing to look at.
  4. Steps may be written before the go, as the plan of the build; none starts until the arc is DECIDED.
  5. Planning jobs fill the preview and the arc’s facts, and the arc stays PROPOSED the whole time. plan.md is not written while an arc is PROPOSED; at the go it is written only where there are traps or a move table.
  6. Each move is told in one line: N002 opened from How: the platform’s screens and flows, with its preview.

How arcs are cut

  1. The edge of an arc is what you review together and what releases together. The domain gives it its name.
  2. A package is released by one arc only. When another arc needs a change in it, the change is a step of the arc that releases it, and the work that needs it waits on that release.
  3. Each package releases after the last step that changes it, not all of them at the end. Where a domain does not release on its own, such as a module inside one app, the arc lands at its proof.
  4. A goal too big to review once is split by when you would review it. If both halves touch one package it releases twice, and if that is not worth it the split is wrong.
  5. A fix to the agent’s machinery, a plugin or the design system outside the goal’s domains goes to the workstream that owns it, or where you say, and the reply links where it went. In a partner’s workspace, where nobody owns the plugin, it becomes an issue the agent drafts for SaaS Plane’s public marketplace repository.

For 030 this gives three arcs where there are ten: Surface (the patterns standard, the design system, the plugin), Platform (the demo site, the screens and the flows), and saasplane.ai.

Placing something new

One order of questions replaces the six tables. The agent reads where the workstream stands first: its goal, which arcs landed, which are building, which wait, and each open arc’s goal. Then it asks, in this order, and stops at the first yes:

  1. Is it a question? It is answered, and nothing opens.
  2. Is it another subject, or outside the goal’s domains? A workstream is suggested, or it goes where § How arcs are cut says.
  3. Does it fall inside an arc that has not landed? The test is whether that arc’s goal already covers it. Yes: a step there, or a section of its preview while it is PROPOSED.
  4. Does it fix what a landed arc delivered? The test is whether the landed arc’s goal would stay word for word as it is. Yes: something it promised does not hold, or needs a polish, so it is a step on the review-fixes arc, naming the arc it fixes.
  5. Otherwise it is new scope, something no arc’s goal promised: a new arc, PROPOSED, named for its domain, with a preview when there is something to see. Its package rule still holds: a change in a package another open arc releases is a step of that arc.

A landed arc is never reopened, because its goal and your review of it are the record of what was delivered. The reply says in one line where the new thing went and why (“a fix to N006’s band buttons, on review fixes: N006’s goal is unchanged”), so you can move it with one word if the agent read it wrongly.

The kinds of go, and the other words that move things

Your words

Create

The workstream, its approach page, and N001 PROPOSED.

For example: “yes, create it”

Go on a preview

Each arc named moves from PROPOSED to DECIDED, and building starts.

For example: “N002’s preview is good to go”, “all arcs are ready”

Wait

The arc is decided and held: the wait is kept with your words, and nothing starts, in this window or the next.

For example: “approved, but wait”, “stop N003”

Start

Clears the wait, and building starts.

For example: “start N003”

An answer

No status moves; the answer goes into What and the preview.

For example: “Q18 A”

A change

A step; a status moves only when you agree an arc’s goal changed.

For example: “fix the footer’s gap”

Drop

An arc never decided is deleted; one decided before becomes DROPPED.

For example: “drop N004”

Move

CARRIED, and its work opens in the other workstream.

For example: “move N004 to 031”

Park

The folder moves to backlog/, with the blocker named.

For example: “park this until the cloud account exists”

A version

The release’s version.

For example: “release it as 6.0.0”

Close

After the review links, the page reads DONE and the folder moves to closed/.

For example: “close it”
  • A go answers only what it names. “Approved” on one arc’s preview decides that arc, not its neighbours and not an open card. Words that name no arc, such as “looks good” while several arcs are PROPOSED, move nothing, and the agent asks which arc.
  • Every go is logged with your words, and the reply says in one line what it moved and what stays open: N002 decided, building started; Q19 still open.

Arc status

Six statuses. Only your words and the steps move them; a planning job, a fact, a preview edit, a card’s answer or a step added inside the arc’s goal never does.

  • A stored PROPOSED wins over the steps: when you agree an arc’s goal changed, anything it was building stops until your next go.
  • LANDED means every step landed, deferred and carried steps left out of the count, and the final proof passed.
  • PART-LANDED and HELD go. A stalled arc shows what it is doing and when it last moved, and a held one shows your wait.
  • The review-fixes arc opens at the first “fix X” after any arc lands, DECIDED on those words, and takes fixes for every arc of the workstream, each saying which arc it fixes. It is the one arc that lands on your word: it reads RUNNING until you close the workstream.

Workstream status

The agent’s steps

You never need these; they are here so the record is whole.

State

waiting · ready

Written; ready once what it waits on has landed, and only on a DECIDED arc with no wait.

running

Started, with the time it started.

stopped

Put down, with what has to happen first: often a card, or a changed goal.

replaced

Started, then replaced by new steps after your change; its words are kept.

landed

In its repository, with its commit and proof.

deferred · carried

Comes back when its event happens · moved to another workstream.

discarded

Found wrong or not needed before it started: it leaves the arc, and the log keeps its words.

Every case, and what the agent does

Each rule is stated once, in its subsection above; this table points to it.

Case

You ask for a new workstream

§ Before a workstream exists.

Status: N001 PROPOSED · page PLANNING

The agent sees another subject while you discuss

It suggests a workstream in one line; at your yes, as above.

Status: none until your yes

The discussion makes things clearer

§ Shaping.

Status: new arcs PROPOSED

You say go, wait, start, drop or move

§ The kinds of go.

Status: as that table says

Your words name no arc while several are PROPOSED

It asks which arc, and moves nothing.

Status: unchanged

You add something while arcs are under review

§ Placing something new: into the matching PROPOSED arc’s preview; on a DECIDED arc, a step when it is inside the goal; outside every goal, a new PROPOSED arc. Told in one line.

Status: unchanged, or a new arc

You ask for a change while an arc is building

Inside the goal, a step. If it changes what is being built right now, the agent stops at the next commit, shows you the new plan in words and resumes. If it thinks the goal moved, it asks you.

Status: unchanged, or PROPOSED at your yes

A card’s answer is needed while building

It stops only the work the answer can change, says in words what waits, and the rest keeps going.

Status: unchanged

An arc has landed and you ask for a fix to it

§ Placing something new: a step on the review-fixes arc, saying which arc it fixes.

Status: review fixes RUNNING; the landed arc stays LANDED

Some arcs have landed and you ask for something bigger

§ Placing something new: same subject, a new arc with a preview if there is something to see; another subject, a workstream suggested.

Status: new arc PROPOSED; page stays IMPLEMENTING

Every arc has landed

It shows you the review links, one per changed app, and waits.

Status: “waiting for your review”

You are not happy with the review

The fixes go on the review-fixes arc.

Status: review fixes RUNNING

You say close

It runs the close gate (§ Workstream status) and moves the folder.

Status: DONE · closed/

You ask a question

It answers it, and opens nothing.

Status: none

A machinery, plugin or design-system fix outside the goal

§ How arcs are cut, the last point.

Status: none here

The work is blocked by something outside the workstream

It says what blocks it and suggests parking; it parks on your word.

Status: folder in backlog/

A window ends while building

The next window resumes from the first step not landed, and keeps any wait you gave.

Status: unchanged

Delegated work takes the light form

Built already, and shown here so the whole way of working is on one page.

  1. A mechanical step, such as a pin move, a rename or a prop swap the brief can list, is done by the agent itself, with no child, brief or report.
  2. A brief names the files to change, the one rule they follow and the acceptance, and nothing else to read first.
  3. A child runs apps check on each node it touched and the specs it changed or added, narrowed. A fail-once proof is only for new behaviour.
  4. Whole test tiers, browser walks and the look run once, at the arc’s final re-check, and you see the look as soon as a batch lands.
  5. Commits are fewer and bigger: each touched tier runs whole once per batch.
  6. A report is at most 15 lines, and a hand-back at most 8.

What each event writes

Event

Create

The folder, the approach page, N001’s record and preview.

An arc opened, merged or re-goaled while planning

The arc’s record and preview, one line in How, one log line.

A go, a wait, a start

One status line with your words.

A step added, started or landed

One record write each, and no page edit.

A card answered

The card’s record, one sentence in What, the preview section it touches.

An arc lands

What brought current in a sentence or two.

Close

The close gate, and the folder move.

Targets, counted again on the next workstream: about three log events per step and three per arc, and for each arc before its go its notes in KB and its planning jobs’ tokens, against what 030’s sizing cost (the measurements are in the arc’s plan).

Where it lands

The book first, then spn-devex and its migration, then one release and a sync of the workspace.
